segments: The tenth dynasty: the Arab kings.
More than the Romans, they were shocked at this bitter breach,
because they used to say that it was written among them
that when Amorium should be breached by them,
their kingdom would come to an end.
And while al-Mu'tasim was occupied with the destruction of Amorium,
'Abbas the son of al-Ma'mun his brother, and 'Ujayf, the commander of the army, were plotting to kill him.
And through a certain scribe and a Nestorian physician, their treachery was revealed.
And the king bound them,
and loaded them onto camels,
and set out from Amorium.
'Abbas, however, died on the way of thirst at Mabbugh.
And al-Mu'tasim wrote to the provinces
that 'Abbas the son of al-Ma'mun should be cursed,
for he had wished to deliver the entire camp of the Arabs into the hands of the Romans.
Now Theophilus, when he saw what the Arabs had done to Amorium,
blamed himself because he was the first who had begun the destruction of Zopetra.
And he sent presents and gifts to al-Mu'tasim with Basil the patrician of Charsianon, and a letter of friendship;
and he asked for Aetios the patrician, who was held captive by the Arabs,
promising that he would give {in return} the Arab captives.
And he also wrote another letter of threats and insults,
{commanding} that if he was not willing for peace,
Basil should deliver it.
And when al-Mu'tasim received the letter of peace,
he demanded that they should give him, along with all the Arab captives, also Nasr the Kurd and Manuel the patrician, who had come to the Arabs and then fled again.
And when Basil answered
that this was impossible,
he said to him:
"Prepare yourselves, then, for war."
Then Basil delivered the letter of threats.
And when it was read, al-Mu'tasim became enraged,
and he returned the gifts of Theophilus to the ambassador, and sent Abu Sa'id to make ambushes in one quarter,
and Bashir the satrap and the people of Mopsuestia in another quarter.
And when Bashir took captives,
Nasr and the Kurds overtook him and rescued the captives.
Then Abu Sa'id arrived,
and the Arabs gained strength and killed Nasr and many of the Kurds.
And they collected many heads,
and salted them,
and brought them to Mopsuestia.
And when the women of Mopsuestia came out to meet their men who had returned, supposedly in victory,
and to gaze in delight upon the heads of the Kurds,
they recognized that many of the heads were those of their own husbands,
since those Kurds, before being defeated, had killed some of the Arabs.
And their joy was turned into mourning.
